questions.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the internal diameter of a test tube?
questions.explanation: A vernier calliper has upper inside jaws designed to grip the inner wall of a tube, and a least count of 0.01 cm which suits a diameter of a few centimetres. No other instrument in the list can reach inside the tube.

distractorRationale.a: A metre rule cannot be placed inside the tube and is only precise to 0.1 cm
distractorRationale.c: A micrometer measures external thickness only; its anvil and spindle cannot fit inside a tube
distractorRationale.d: A measuring cylinder measures volume of liquid, not length

questions.stem: What is the least count of a standard micrometer screw gauge?
questions.explanation: One complete turn of the thimble moves the spindle 0.5 mm, and the thimble carries 50 divisions, so one division corresponds to $\frac{0.5}{50} = 0.01\ \text{mm}$. This is why the micrometer is used for thin wires and sheets.

distractorRationale.a: This is roughly the least count of a metre rule
distractorRationale.b: 0.10 mm is the least count of a vernier calliper, ten times coarser
distractorRationale.d: 0.01 cm equals 0.1 mm, again the vernier calliper value

questions.stem: A student wishes to find the thickness of a single sheet of exercise-book paper. The best method is to

options.text: measure one sheet with a metre rule
measure the thickness of 100 sheets with a micrometer and divide by 100
measure one sheet with a measuring cylinder
measure one sheet with a spring balance

questions.explanation: A single sheet is far thinner than the least count of any school instrument, so measuring one sheet gives a huge percentage error. Stacking 100 sheets multiplies the quantity being measured by 100 while the instrument's uncertainty stays the same, so dividing at the end gives a far more reliable value.

distractorRationale.a: A metre rule reads only to 1 mm, which is many times the thickness of one sheet
distractorRationale.c: A measuring cylinder measures volume, not thickness
distractorRationale.d: A spring balance measures force, not length

questions.stem: On a vernier calliper of least count 0.01 cm, the vernier zero lies just beyond the 2.6 cm mark of the main scale and the 7th vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. Calculate the reading. Give your answer in centimetres.
questions.explanation: Main scale reading is 2.6 cm. Vernier scale reading is $7 \times 0.01 = 0.07\ \text{cm}$. The total reading is $2.6 + 0.07 = 2.67\ \text{cm}$, quoted to two decimal places because that is the precision of the instrument.

questions.stem: The sleeve scale of a micrometer screw gauge reads 7.5 mm and the thimble reads 18 divisions. Calculate the diameter of the rod being measured. Give your answer in millimetres.
questions.explanation: Sleeve reading is 7.5 mm, including the exposed half-millimetre mark. Thimble contribution is $18 \times 0.01 = 0.18\ \text{mm}$. Total diameter $= 7.5 + 0.18 = 7.68\ \text{mm}$.

questions.stem: With its jaws fully closed a micrometer screw gauge reads +0.03 mm. It is then used on a wire and reads 1.25 mm. The true diameter of the wire is
questions.explanation: The instrument has a positive zero error of 0.03 mm, meaning every reading is 0.03 mm too large. Subtract it: $1.25 - 0.03 = 1.22\ \text{mm}$.

distractorRationale.c: Adds the zero error instead of subtracting it — that correction is only for a negative zero error
distractorRationale.d: Quotes the zero error itself rather than the corrected diameter

questions.stem: The volume of a small irregular stone is best found by

options.text: measuring its longest side with a vernier calliper and cubing it
weighing it on a beam balance
lowering it into a measuring cylinder of water and noting the rise in level
measuring its thickness with a micrometer screw gauge

questions.explanation: An irregular solid has no formula for its volume, so we use displacement: the stone pushes aside a volume of water exactly equal to its own volume, and the rise in the water level reads that volume directly.

distractorRationale.a: Cubing one side only works for a cube; an irregular stone is not a cube
distractorRationale.b: A beam balance gives mass, and you would still need the density to get volume
distractorRationale.d: A micrometer gives a single thickness, which tells you nothing about total volume

questions.stem: Which pair of instruments measures mass and weight respectively?
questions.explanation: A beam balance compares the unknown mass with standard masses, so it gives mass and reads the same anywhere in the universe. A spring balance measures the pull of gravity by how far a spring stretches, so it gives weight in newtons and would read less on the Moon.

distractorRationale.a: The two instruments are the right ones but in the wrong order
distractorRationale.c: A measuring cylinder measures volume, not weight
distractorRationale.d: A vernier calliper measures length, not weight

questions.stem: A vernier scale has 20 divisions which together span exactly 19 mm of the main scale, whose smallest division is 1 mm. Calculate the least count of this calliper. Give your answer in millimetres.
questions.explanation: Least count equals one main-scale division minus one vernier-scale division. One vernier division is $\frac{19}{20} = 0.95\ \text{mm}$, so the least count is $1 - 0.95 = 0.05\ \text{mm}$. Equivalently, least count $= \frac{\text{smallest main division}}{\text{number of vernier divisions}} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05\ \text{mm}$.

questions.stem: In a pendulum experiment a student times 20 complete oscillations rather than one. The main reason is to

options.text: make the pendulum swing more regularly
reduce the percentage error caused by reaction time
increase the period of the pendulum
remove the zero error of the stopwatch

questions.explanation: Starting and stopping a stopwatch introduces an uncertainty of roughly 0.2 s no matter how long the interval is. That 0.2 s is about 10% of a 2 s single swing but only about 0.5% of a 40 s run of twenty swings, so dividing the total by 20 gives a much more accurate period.

distractorRationale.a: The regularity of the swing depends on the length and the amplitude, not on how the timing is done
distractorRationale.c: The period is fixed by the pendulum length; timing more swings does not change it
distractorRationale.d: Repeating swings does not correct a zero error; only resetting or subtracting it does

distractorRationale.d: A measuring tape is generally used for larger measurements and lacks precision for small objects.
